name: Quechua de Aurahuá-Chupamarca
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Gálvez Astorayme, Isabel. 2008. Esbozo fonológico del quechua de Aurahuá-Chupamarca. Boletín de la Academia Peruana de la Lengua 46(46): 49-72. DOI 10.46744/bapl.200802.003 (open access, CC BY 4.0).
catalog_quote: 2. El acento. El acento en el quechua de Aurahuá-Chupamarca no es una propiedad fonémica; es decir, no es de carácter léxico. Esta afirmación supone que el acento en el quechua de Aurahuá-Chupamarca sigue el patrón de acentuación regular de la gran mayoría de variedades; por consiguiente, se desprende de esta afirmación que el patrón acentual es claramente predecible (grave). Presentamos una pequeña lista de datos para dar cuenta de la acentuación grave del quechua de esta zona: [kánaŋ] 'ahora', [ášna-] 'apestar', [sápra] 'barba', [úma] 'cabeza', [máska-] 'buscar', [máray] 'batán'. ... [preceding paragraph, same page:] Por otro lado, aun cuando la cantidad vocálica es una propiedad léxica, la disposición de tales segmentos es sumamente restringida, ya que la encontramos preferentemente en voces bisilábicas y, únicamente en la primera sílaba empezando de la izquierda. A continuación, presentamos nuevamente los casos expuestos anteriormente: /sa:pi/ [sá:pi] 'raíz', /ti:pa/ [tí:pa] 'prendedor', /a:nas/ [á:nas] 'zorrino'.

new_statements.translation: 2. Stress. Stress in the Quechua of Aurahuá-Chupamarca is not a phonemic property; that is, it is not lexical. This statement implies that stress in Aurahuá-Chupamarca Quechua follows the regular accentuation pattern of the great majority of [Quechua] varieties; consequently it follows that the stress pattern is clearly predictable (paroxytone, i.e. penultimate). We give a short list of data to illustrate the penultimate ('grave') accentuation of the Quechua of this area: [kánaŋ] 'now', [ášna-] 'to stink', [sápra] 'beard', [úma] 'head', [máska-] 'to look for', [máray] 'grinding stone'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable: it falls on the penultimate syllable of the word ('acentuación grave'), as in most Quechua varieties. Lexical vowel length exists but is confined to the first syllable of (mostly) disyllabic roots and is described independently of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned by Gálvez 2008 (examples are all di- and trisyllabic roots; no discussion of suffixed words, exclamations, or long-vowel person marking). For the neighbouring Southern Yauyos varieties that include San Pedro de Huacarpana (Chincha), Shimelman 2017:23 adds: exclamations often final-stressed; final stress when a 1st-person long vowel is word-final; weak stress on the first syllable of words longer than four syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement illustrated with isolated citation forms (bare roots, including verb roots cited with a hyphen); no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Quechua of the districts of Aurahuá and Chupamarca (Castrovirreyna province, Huancavelica), a quantity-insensitive/QII 'border dialect'; Glottolog files it under chin1483 with language code 'Arma-Aurahuá-Chupamarca = Chincha Quechua [qxc]'. ISO qxc / Ethnologue 'Chincha Quechua' proper refers to the adjacent north-eastern Chincha-province districts (Chavín de Topará, San Juan de Yanac, San Pedro de Huacarpana, Ica region). San Pedro de Huacarpana is also covered by Shimelman 2017 (Southern Yauyos Quechua, yauy1235), which likewise states penultimate stress (p. 23). No description devoted specifically to Topará/Chavín Quechua was found.

sources.note: Sec. 2 'El acento', p. 63: stress is not phonemic/lexical; it follows the regular pattern of the great majority of Quechua varieties and is clearly predictable, 'grave' (= penultimate); examples [kánaŋ] 'ahora', [ášna-] 'apestar', [sápra] 'barba', [úma] 'cabeza', [máska-] 'buscar', [máray] 'batán'. Vowel length is lexical but restricted to the first syllable of (mostly) disyllables (p. 62-63). Nothing on secondary stress or exceptions.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2 p. 23 (for Southern Yauyos Quechua, yauy1235, whose corpus includes San Pedro de Huacarpana in Chincha province, i.e. inside ISO qxc territory; pp. 5-12 discuss Chincha's Topará and Huacarpana classification): 'primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a word'; first syllable of words of more than four syllables gets weak stress; exceptions: exclamations often final-stressed, and in dialects marking 1st person by vowel length stress is final when that long vowel is word-final.
